newsitem.title: USA: U.S. battle lines drawn on late-term abortions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. battle lines drawn on late-term abortions.

text.p: Battle lines were drawn on Tuesday on the contentious issue of so-called partial-birth abortion, with abortion rights proponents hoping to keep the procedure legal and Senate Republicans vowing to ban it.

One day after the scripted amity of President Bill Clinton's second inauguration and one day before the 24th anniversary of the Supreme Court's landmark Roe v. Wade ruling, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott made banning the rare late-term abortions a top legislative priority.

"Partial birth abortion ban -- the president vetoed that bill last year," the Mississippi Republican told a news conference unveiling his party's top 10 goals for the new congressional session. "We think this is a shameless act that we must deal with ... we are determined to do this. And we will do it earlier rather than later in this first session."

At a separate news conference, Kate Michelman, head of the National Abortion and Reproductive Rights Action League, said the right to this kind of abortion, under attack in the Republican-led Congress, would likely be preserved.

Clinton, a Democrat who has consistently favoured abortion rights, vetoed a bill last year that would have banned the procedure and the Senate was unable to override the veto. But Lott said Clinton had indicated a willingness to discuss the measure, and Michelman said she was aware of plans to try to make the bill more palatable to the president.
"I think we can still retain a presidential veto," Michelman said, but she added, "We have a tough Senate to deal with. It's not easy but I think we can do that."

So-called partial-birth abortion, technically called dilation and evacuation, is sometimes used in late-term abortions. Under the technique, a foetus is partially delivered feet first until just the head remains in the birth canal, the brains are then suctioned out and the skull collapsed.

Last year's legislation was the first time Congress moved to ban a specific abortion procedure rather than dealing with the general issue of abortion rights. In vetoing the bill Clinton said he had concerns about the procedure but could not sign it because it did not include constitutional protections for a woman's health.

Michelman said while abortion rights activists had been "elated" when Clinton was elected in 1992, much of the progress made on abortion rights in the first two years of his presidency was eroded after Republican majorities were elected in 1994 in both houses of Congress.

Michelman's group on Tuesday reported on increasing restrictions on access to abortion, saying 12 states enforce three or more restrictions on abortion services, as compared with just two states in 1990.

The study was timed to coincide with Wednesday's anniversary of the Supreme Court's 1973 decision in Roe v. Wade, which held that the constitutional right to privacy gave women the right to choose an abortion. The date is often a flashpoint for people on both sides of the debate and this year was preceded by bombings at abortion clinics in Atlanta last Tuesday and Tulsa, Oklahoma, on Sunday.

The Catholic Church planned a mass and prayer vigil Tuesday evening at the Basilica of the Shrine of the Immaculate Conception, the largest U.S. Catholic church, "in thanksgiving for the gift of human life," according to a statement released by the church's Washington headquarters.
